title: How I Paid Off $41,000 in Student Loans in 3 Years
creator: Nadia Brooks
description:
Three years, two jobs, one very ugly spreadsheet. Here's exactly how I did it, including the parts that didn't work.

sentences.t: In May of 2022 I graduated with a master's degree and forty-one thousand dollars in student loans.
Last month, I made the final payment.
I cried in my car in a grocery store parking lot, which, if you've been there, you understand.
So today I want to walk you through exactly what I did, because I think a lot of the advice out there is either really vague or kind of unrealistic.
First, some context, because it matters.
My starting salary was fifty-four thousand a year, which is not nothing, but it's not tech money either.
I lived in Columbus, which is a pretty affordable city.
And I had no kids, no car payment, and a very tolerant roommate.
If your situation is different, some of this won't apply, and that's okay.
Step one was honestly just looking at the number.
For the first six months after graduating, I didn't log into my loan account at all, because I was scared of it.
When I finally did, I had six different loans at interest rates from about four to almost seven percent.
I tracked every one of them in a Google Sheets spreadsheet, nothing fancy, just the balance, the rate and the minimum payment.
It's the same free spreadsheet I'd used for group projects in grad school, I just added a tab and color coded it way too much.
Step two, I picked a method and stuck to it.
I went with the avalanche method, which means you pay the minimum on everything, and every extra dollar goes to the highest interest loan first.
Mathematically it saves you the most money.
Emotionally, it can be brutal, because that first loan takes forever to disappear.
If you need quick wins to stay motivated, the snowball method, smallest balance first, is completely fine too.
The best method is the one you don't quit.
Step three was the budget, and this is where I made my biggest mistake.
My first budget was way too strict.
No eating out, no new clothes, nothing fun at all, and I lasted about seven weeks before I blew two hundred dollars at Target out of pure frustration.
So I rebuilt it with a small fun budget, a hundred dollars a month that was mine to waste, no guilt.
And weirdly, that's when it started working.
Step four, the income side.
Cutting costs only gets you so far, and at some point you have to earn more.
I tutored high school chemistry two evenings a week, which brought in about six hundred dollars a month.
And in year two I negotiated a raise by bringing a list of every project I'd led, which got me to sixty-one thousand.
Every single dollar of the raise went to the loans, I pretended it didn't exist.
So, the timeline.
Year one I paid off about nine thousand, which felt like nothing.
Year two, about fourteen.
And year three, with the raise and the tutoring, I paid the last eighteen thousand in eleven months.
Was it worth it?
For me, yes, but I'll be honest, I missed a lot of trips and a couple of weddings.
If your interest rates are low, it might make more sense to pay the minimum and invest the difference, and there's no shame in that.
Next week I'm going to talk about what I'm doing with that payment money now, because it's a weird feeling having it back.
Let me know in the comments where you are in your own debt journey, I read all of them.
Bye for now.
